title: Documenting Authentication and Errors
learning_outcomes: Explain how documenting authentication and errors affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from security schemes to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on documenting authentication and errors in api contracts and documentation. You will connect security schemes to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Documenting Authentication and Errors matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying security schemes deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Lesson 140 concept map

content_blocks.caption: Follow the 4 syllabus topics in order, then inspect the example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: An OpenAPI description is a machine-readable contract; it should match implemented methods, schemas, security, and errors. In this lesson, treat “Documenting Authentication and Errors” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: Documenting Authentication and Errors
content_blocks.code:
openapi: 3.1.2
info:
  title: Task API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /v1/tasks:
    get:
      operationId: listTasks
      responses:
        "200":
          description: A bounded page of tasks
content_blocks.expected_output: This compact OpenAPI fragment describes an operation and a response contract. Validate the full document with tooling compatible with the declared OpenAPI version.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Security schemes”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Operation-level security requirements” and “Shared error schemas and examples”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: The contract should explain successful requests, failures, authentication, schemas, and compatibility. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating documenting authentication and errors. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Security schemes” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Documenting Authentication and Errors with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating documenting authentication and errors as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: An OpenAPI description is a machine-readable contract; it should match implemented methods, schemas, security, and errors. In this lesson, treat “Documenting Authentication and Errors” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
Next, connect this idea to Lesson 141: Reusable OpenAPI Components.
